title: Many-Child Tree to Text and Back
statement:
A tree where each node can have any number of children, in a fixed order, must be saved as one string and later rebuilt from that string alone. Think of saving a nested menu or a folder tree. Design two functions:

  • serialize(root) turns the tree into a single string, in any format you like.
  • deserialize(data) receives only that string and rebuilds a tree with exactly the same shape, values and child order.

Values may repeat, and the tree may be empty.

How it is tested. The runner passes the tree as nested arrays: a node is [value, [child, child, …]], a leaf is [value, []] and the empty tree is null. Implement roundTrip(root): convert the arrays into node objects { val, children }, run deserialize(serialize(node)), and convert the rebuilt nodes back to nested arrays. A test passes when the result equals the input. Returning the input unchanged would also pass, so the tests cannot hold you to the rules; the exercise is the two helpers, and deserialize may use nothing except the string.

examples.why: The values in pre-order are 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 4, but that alone does not say whether 4 is a child of 3 or of 1. The string must record where each child list ends.
A chain of three 7s has the same values. Repeated values mean the shape cannot be recovered from the values themselves.
The empty tree needs an encoding of its own and must come back as no tree at all.

constraints: The tree is at most 300 levels deep
deserialize may only use the string returned by serialize
hints: Pre-order values alone are ambiguous, because you cannot tell where one node's children stop. What extra number or marker per node would fix that?
Option one: write each node as its value followed by its number of children, in pre-order. Reading back, a node reads its value and count, then reads exactly that many subtrees.
Option two: walk level by level and after each node's children write an end marker such as #. Reading back, a queue of parents hands out the children up to each marker.

explain.intuition:
For a binary tree you write a marker for each missing child, because every node has exactly two slots. A many-child tree has no fixed number of slots, so the string must say how many children each node has or where each child list ends. The simplest fix: write every node as value, child count in pre-order. Example one becomes 1,3,2,0,3,2,5,0,6,0,4,0.

Reading it back mirrors the writing. A recursive reader with one shared position takes a value and a count, then reads exactly count subtrees as the children, in order. Nothing is ambiguous, because each count tells the reader precisely when to return to the parent. It is the same idea as a length prefix in a binary file format. A level-order version works too: write each node's children followed by an end marker #, and rebuild with a queue that gives children to parents in order.
steps: serialize: pre-order walk; for each node append its value and then its number of children; join with commas. The empty tree becomes the empty string.
deserialize: return null for the empty string. Otherwise split on commas and keep an index i = 0.
read(): create a node from tokens[i++], read count = tokens[i++], then call read() count times and append each result to the node's children.
pitfalls: Writing only the values. The first example and a tree where 4 hangs under 3 would give the same string.
Reading one character per value. 10000 is five characters; split on a delimiter.
Forgetting a distinct encoding for the empty tree, so that null and a single node become confused.

complexity.space: O(n) for the string, O(depth) recursion

solutions.title: Pre-order with child counts
solutions.idea: Write value and child count for every node in pre-order. The reader takes a value and a count, then reads exactly that many subtrees.

solutions.title: Level order with end-of-children markers
solutions.idea: Walk breadth-first and write each node's children followed by #. Rebuild with a queue: each parent in turn takes the values up to the next #.

followups: Make the string as short as possible when most nodes are leaves.
Encode the many-child tree as a binary tree (first child, next sibling) and reuse a binary serializer. How do you decode it?
